title: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top of n stairs?

s1_definition.oneliner: The number of ways to reach step i is the sum of the ways to reach step i-1 (single step) and step i-2 (double step) : it is the Fibonacci sequence.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Recurrence** – `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]`, because the last move is either a single step from i-1 or a double step from i-2.
- **Base cases** – `dp[0] = 1` (one way to stand at ground) and `dp[1] = 1` (one way to reach step 1).
- **Fibonacci identity** – the sequence of way-counts is exactly the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one index.
- **Rolling variables** – since dp[i] depends only on the previous two, two variables replace the array.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space with rolling variables.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer at the National Bank of India climbs a loyalty rewards tier ladder one or two tiers at a time. The number of distinct paths to reach tier 5 is the number of paths to tier 4 (then step one) plus the number of paths to tier 3 (then step two). This builds the Fibonacci sequence tier by tier.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Climbing Stairs is the gateway dynamic programming problem, and it is Fibonacci in disguise. The number of distinct ways to reach step i is the sum of the ways to reach step i-1 (from which you take a single step) and the ways to reach step i-2 (from which you take a double step). Those two sets of paths are disjoint and together cover every possibility, giving the recurrence dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].

The base cases are one way to be at the ground and one way to reach the first step. Because each value depends only on the previous two, you keep two rolling variables instead of a full array, which gives linear time and constant space. The naive recursive version recomputes subproblems exponentially, which is the textbook illustration of why DP exists.

At the National Bank of India, a loyalty tier ladder let members advance one or two tiers per qualifying action, and marketing wanted the count of distinct progression paths to a target tier. The rolling Fibonacci computation answered it instantly. For a k-step variant where members can jump up to k tiers, the recurrence generalises to summing the previous k values.

The senior insight is that Climbing Stairs is a template for all linear recurrence problems: decode ways, tiling, and tribonacci all follow the same "sum the last k results" pattern. For very large n, matrix exponentiation computes the Fibonacci in O(log n) time. Recognising this Fibonacci structure and reducing space with rolling variables is what interviewers expect.

Remember one sentence: Climbing Stairs is Fibonacci: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], and rolling two variables gives O(n) time and O(1) space.

---

keyPoints: Recurrence is dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], identical to the Fibonacci sequence.
Base cases are dp[0] = 1 (ground) and dp[1] = 1 (first step).
Rolling two variables reduces space from O(n) to O(1).
Naive recursion is O(2^n) due to overlapping subproblems.
Generalises to k-step Fibonacci by summing the previous k values.
For very large n, matrix exponentiation gives O(log n) time.
